h1: Tree planting in Longview & East Texas

answer: Yard Dog Landscapes is a family-owned crew in Longview, TX, founded in 2017 and rated 5.0 stars across {{REVIEWS}} Google reviews. We help you pick a tree that fits the soil, the sun and the mature size of the spot, then plant it with the root flare at grade, a wide and shallow hole, a mulch ring and a watering plan. Cost depends on the species, size and number of trees and on site access, so we quote after a free walkthrough. Send a quote request and we'll get back to you within a day.
overview: Planting too deep is the most common way we see a new tree killed in East Texas, and it takes two or three years to finish the job, so nobody traces it back to planting day. We set the root flare, where the trunk widens into its first roots, at grade or an inch above. On container trees that flare is often buried a few inches under the potting soil, so we measure to the flare, not the top of the pot.

The hole is two to three times the width of the root ball and no deeper than the ball is tall, because roots here run sideways. Native soil goes back in, since a pocket of bagged soil in clay holds water like a bathtub. We cut circling roots, build a watering basin, lay a mulch ring pulled back off the trunk, and stake only on windy, exposed sites. Stock comes from regional growers.

timing: Fall is the best window in East Texas, from September until around Thanksgiving. The soil stays warm for weeks after the air cools, so a tree planted in October gets close to six months of root growth before summer, while one planted in April gets about eight weeks. We plant year-round, but a spring tree needs more watering through its first summer.

east_texas.title: A new tree drinks from its root ball, not your yard
text: A container tree comes in a ball of light potting mix. Your yard is clay, or sandy loam over clay. Water doesn't move well between textures that different, so until roots grow out into native soil, the tree is drinking from a buried pot. In July that ball dries out in about a day and a half while the clay six inches away is still moist.

That is why spring trees die in August in yards that got watered. Soak the ball itself with a hose on a trickle for twenty minutes. For a fall tree, do it twice a week for six weeks, weekly through November, then every ten to fourteen days in a dry winter. Soak everything new the day before a hard freeze.

faq.q: When is the best time to plant a tree in East Texas?
faq.a: Fall, from September until around Thanksgiving. The soil stays warm long after the air cools, so roots keep growing through most of our winter, and the tree has months of root under it before the first 100-degree day. Spring planting works but needs more watering all summer. Bare-root fruit trees and roses go in while dormant, December through February.

faq.q: What trees grow best in East Texas?
faq.a: Live oak, Shumard oak, post oak, southern magnolia, bald cypress, red maple, river birch, Chinese pistache, redbud, hollies and crepe myrtles all do well here. What struggles are maples bred for the Midwest and fruit trees from cooler climates. Mature size matters as much as species. A Natchez crepe myrtle wants 25 to 30 feet, while an Acoma stays near 10.

faq.q: Should I add garden soil to the hole when I plant a tree?
faq.a: No. Native soil goes back in the hole. A pocket of bagged garden soil in the middle of clay acts like a bathtub: water runs in, doesn't drain out, and roots circle in the soft pocket instead of growing into the yard. We also skip fertilizer at planting, because nitrogen pushes top growth when you want everything going into roots.

faq.q: Should I buy a bigger tree so I get shade faster?
faq.a: Usually not. A seven-gallon tree planted in October typically passes a thirty-gallon tree planted the same day within about four years, because it establishes faster and never spends a summer in shock. Bigger trees cost more, need more water and take longer to root out. We'll size the tree to the spot and to how long you're willing to wait.
